parts:
Thanks for the simplified example.

I think this works.

I think the key is to have rows for all the combinations
of type and Gender with NA values, so I pre-summarise the data
and join the summary with a data.frame of all the combinations
before plotting.

There might be an easier or more elegant way to do it directly
in ggplot, but I'll leave that to someone else.

Hope this helps,
Ron.



library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)

Gender = c(1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2)
Ageatsurgery = c(61, 62, 62, 62, 62, 62)
type = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 3)
reprex.6 <- data.frame(Gender, Ageatsurgery, type)

#
# Make all combinations
all <- expand.grid(type = c(1, 3), Gender = c(1, 2))
#
# Pre-summarise data
rr <- reprex.6 %>%
group_by(type, Gender, add = FALSE) %>%
summarise(mean = mean(Ageatsurgery)) %>%
full_join(.,all)
#> Joining, by = c("type", "Gender")
ggplot(rr, aes(x = factor(type), y = mean, fill = factor(Gender))) +
geom_bar(stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge')
#> Warning: Removed 1 rows containing missing values (geom_bar).

messages.subject: Re: width of bar when other level of variable is 0
parts:
> Thanks! I'll have to study up on relational database stuff on R, join
> etc. and see if I can make it work on a large dataset.

The join isn't using a relational database, it is just using that
terminology to describe combining two data sets. I used the full_join
function from dplyr, but you could have achieved the same with merge
from base R.

I'm trying to get up to speed with the tidyverse approach to data
handling as it seems appealing, so my example code may have flipped
between tidyverse and base R a bit.

Ron.
